Thanks everyone for joining."},{"id":"M1:T2","text":"So, quick background. XML Services are infrastructure services for mission and support applications, built on XML technology. The idea is they isolate the vendor-unique implementations of data access, so applications don't end up depending on physical access models. And they also give you data management functions for getting at distributed database management systems, local and remote, as one of the solutions for interoperability."},{"id":"M1:T3","text":"Great. Let's start with required states and modes. What modes does the system need to operate in?"},{"id":"M1:T4","text":"First one is what we call Environmental Mode. That's the real-time operations, which have to react to varying degrees of readiness, all the way up to full scale wartime operations, things like crisis planning. And that's using heterogeneous data types and sources, transfer capabilities, and data management services."},{"id":"M1:T5","text":"Also on COE compliance, XML Services have to be segmented, and the COE sponsors need to stick to the compliance level requirements in the I&RTS."},{"id":"M1:T6","text":"Then there's the fixed, or static, mode, so a base or a data processing megacenter. There the data management services have to be tunable by on-site personnel, to adjust for varying workloads and sizes of the associated databases. And we expect those workloads and databases to change more often and more significantly than with the processing for deployed units. Now in a changing, dynamic environment, like deployed units, workload and database sizes may be more predetermined, because the mission's more precise, and they'd need access to fewer data management admin capabilities than a fixed environment. And the XS has to be able to redefine or reset names of connect descriptors to database server instances. Right?"},{"id":"M1:T8","text":"Yes, that's right."},{"id":"M1:T9","text":"From the user side, there's degraded communications. If users hitting the data management services are affected by degraded comms, we need, for example, to be able to reset session time-out values. At minimum those time-out values have to be user definable and resettable before a user session is initialized. The goal is having the option to change session time values dynamically, based on current communications performance as identified by network management or the DBMS. Then there's End User Mode. Part of the XS services will be used by different classes of users: data consumers, data and database managers, and network information infrastructure resource managers. Some of those uses come with unique requirements, and those have to be fulfilled within what XS services can do."},{"id":"M1:T10","text":"Then Maintenance Mode. That covers modifying or adding application data segments, user permissions, privileges, and restructuring storage and memory areas. Maintenance also covers shutdown, open not-mounted, and online or off-line implementations, modifications, upgrades, or related actions. And the data management services have to support managing various types of data, database architectures and platforms, hardware and software, at the specified sites. Last is Training Mode. For training, the data management services should give the same processing you'd see in production. The difference is database access may come through a training application accessing the DBMS rather than the production mission application."},{"id":"M1:T11","text":"Got it."},{"id":"M1:T12","text":"Okay, moving on to the XML services capability requirements. What does the XS need to deliver overall?"},{"id":"M1:T13","text":"At a high level, the XS delivers a set of inter-related components, the ones shown in figure 3.2-1."},{"id":"M1:T14","text":"And registering terms and structures, so tags, DTDs, DCDs. How should that work?"},{"id":"M1:T15","text":"So first, producer services. A producer is an agent contributing metadata to an XML Registry, so a term gets maximum semantic understanding as it appears in an XML document. To contribute, the producer has to be able to receive XML registry forms, submit metadata and the related information resource artifacts, and notify. We need to produce and display submittal forms as part of the Information Resource Submittal Package from the web, with these artifacts: XML Tag Specification, XML Spec, meaning DTD, DCD and so on, and a sample XML document of the tag being submitted. That package gets compressed and emailed or sent by ftp to an addressee. Users download the Submittal Package from the web, which has forms, instructions, and tools for submitting to the XML Registry. They submit prescribed metadata on information resource type, information resource association, status code, data types specified, and the other info specified in Appendix A, across a combination of forms. Those forms are part of that same package, same artifacts: XML Tag Specification, XML Spec like DTD or DCD, and the sample XML document, again compressed and emailed or ftp'd to an addressee. Submission can be an on-line interactive process or an off-line and interactive batch process. Then the system parses submitted XML Registry specification forms and populates the XML Registry database. We need to modify specified terms and definitions of metadata and status of Information Resources, associate Information Resources as in Appendix A, and annotate rejected ones, that one's still a question mark. Assemble registered information resources into new components, assemble new DTDs from current ones, and produce a DTD as an instantiation for the modeling environment, the others being database schema and message definition. Notify on changes in Information Resources or the authorized producer of a tag. Provide a capability to post planned changes to a registry, approve and reject submissions, and forward requests to a different registry."},{"id":"M1:T16","text":"Then consumer services. A consumer looks through a registry to pick a tag structure to reuse in one or more applications that exchange data under a pre-defined agreement. For discovery, they view XML Tags with these relationships: ancestor/descendant, to see a tag's origin; uses/used by, to see a complex Container Tag's parent/child relationship; data type information, a tag's data type and related info; versioning, an Information Resource's versions; reference sets, text related to the domain values or related reference set; and amplifying information, other resources like ERwin models, DTDs, documents and so on. They can view tags in a tree or hierarchy structure or tabular format, with multiple search options to find a specific tag, and a search to find all tags of a given subscriber or author. Each Information Resource gets its own web page showing all pertinent info according to its type. They can view the Submittal Package with the XML Tag Specification, XML Spec like DTD or DCD, and the sample XML document. Display an XML Tag Specification form to the author of an information resource, used for inputting the requested info for that resource. Download the XML Tags or other selected Information Resources. Catalog entities and attributes within servers so you can browse, search and retrieve data related to XML sources. Process ANSI standard SQL as specified in FIPS PUB 127-2. Establish rules to ensure maximum semantic understanding of a term as it appears in an XML document. Links to DTDs, DCDs, and Namespace. And a capability to subscribe for notification of changes to Communities of Interest, COE, or Information Resources."},{"id":"M1:T17","text":"Okay."},{"id":"M1:T18","text":"And there's consuming XML and schema documents.
